Surprise is a sudden disruption of expectation. It occurs when an event happens that the audience did not anticipate, often shifting the direction of the scene in an instant. It provides a shock, but because it arrives without warning, it offers no opportunity for the audience to react before the moment has passed.

Suspense, by contrast, is the tension that comes from expectation. It exists when the audience knows something that the characters do not—or when they understand the consequences of a looming event that the characters have yet to face. Suspense requires information; it gives the audience the burden of anticipation, forcing them to wait for the inevitable moment when the unknown becomes known.

In short, surprise is the moment the bomb goes off; suspense is the audience watching the clock tick down while the character remains unaware of the device beneath the table.
